title: Tearful Jack Draper out of Canadian Open as chronic elbow injury appears to cause more pain
content:
When Jack Draper fired a first serve wide and the speed gun made its determination, the concern began. A 96 mph delivery was a clue that the chronic bone bruising in his left elbow, which has hampered Draper’s tennis since the 2025 clay-court season, had flared again.

Three points later, France’s Térence Atmane cracked a forehand past a stationary Draper to move up 6-3, 2-6, 4-1 in their first-round match at the ATP Masters 1000 Canadian Open in Montreal, seemingly putting the result beyond doubt. As Draper sat at the side of the court for the change of ends and stared at the floor, tears began to flow.

Atmane, the 24-year-old world No. 46 from France, completed a 6-3, 2-6, 6-2 win with a minimum of fuss two games later, and Draper’s latest attempt to return to the court was over.

The 24-year-old Briton, who has a career-high ranking of world No. 4 and won the prestigious BNP Paribas Open at Indian Wells, Calif., in 2024, has to play competitive tennis matches to find out if his playing arm is ready to withstand that competition. To play competitive matches, he has to practice at match intensity — which can cause the elbow to flare up. That ebb and flow was behind his last-minute withdrawal from last week’s D.C. Open in Washington, which would have been Draper’s first tournament since the Eastbourne Open, a grass-court tuneup for Wimbledon.

Draper reached the semifinals of that event, but he then withdrew from his home Grand Slam on its opening day, 24 hours before he was scheduled to play Taylor Fritz of the U.S. in a blockbuster first-round encounter.

At its worst, Draper’s elbow injury kept him out between August 2025, when he withdrew from the U.S. Open after winning his first-round match, and February this year. On his return to Indian Wells, Draper defeated Novak Djokovic in a high-quality three-set match, but lost to finalist Daniil Medvedev in the next round before losing his opening match at the Miami Open.

He then had to retire from the Barcelona Open with a tendon issue in his right knee, which kept him out of the French Open.

At Wimbledon, Draper described the elbow injury as “extremely complicated” in a news conference.

“It’s one of those, it’s hard to tell when you can push, when not to push,” he said.

Draper also discussed the mental toll of his persistent injuries, which have dogged him on and off for the last few years, and spoke about working with a sports psychologist.

“You have something that stops you in your tracks when you’re not expecting it. I think it’s really difficult to accept that, especially after coming through what you’ve come through in the past,” he said.

He echoed those sentiments in an interview with the ATP Tour’s Tennis TV ahead of the Canadian Open.

“Everyone around me is doing everything we can to help this keep moving along … But it’s not as simple as rest and heal up and you’ll come back and you’ll be fine,” he said.

Draper will aim to play at the Cincinnati Open, which starts Aug. 13. He has received a wild card, just as he did to enter the Canadian Open, with his ranking having dropped to world No. 143 thanks to his missing so many events due to injury.
